title: Costilla County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Costilla County wells have a 170 ft median depth and 10 gpm median yield. See what that means for drilling cost, water levels, and buying land.
h1: Water wells in Costilla County, Colorado
intro_html:
Costilla County wells are all over the map, from shallow alluvial holes to deep fractured-bedrock completions. County-wide records show a 170 foot median depth and a 10 gallon-per-minute median yield, which is solid for rural Colorado. But there are also wells over 1,000 feet and a small share with marginal production.

If you’re looking at land around places like Fort Garland, Blanca, San Luis, or San Acacio, the permit data tells you what to expect for depth, water level, and drilling cost before you commit.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Costilla County
sections.html:
Across Costilla County, the median well depth is 170 feet, with the middle half between 100 and 280 feet. About 24% of wells are under 100 feet, and 53% fall between 100 and 300 feet, so most domestic wells don’t require extreme depth. Another 20% run 300–600 feet, and a small 3% go beyond 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 1,325 feet.

For a driller’s bid, this spread means you plan around that 100–280 foot band but know you could land in the deeper group if you’re in tougher fractured-bedrock zones. Checking nearby permits on your parcel is the best way to narrow that down before you budget.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you usually get
sections.html:
Yield in Costilla County is generally favorable. The median reported pump rate is 10 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 7 and 15 gpm. That’s more than enough for a typical exempt household well and normal indoor use plus some outdoor watering, within Colorado’s legal limits.

Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 8% sit in the 1–5 gpm range, which are the ones you treat with caution. Most wells, 64%, produce 5–15 gpm, and 28% are over 15 gpm. So the odds are in your favor, but you still confirm nearby yields instead of assuming every hole will be strong.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend
sections.html:
Static water levels, where they’re reported, have a median of 80 feet below the surface, with the middle half between 45 and 160 feet. That’s the depth to water, not total well depth, and it affects pump setting and energy use more than drilling cost itself.

Looking at measurements by decade, the median water level was about 85 feet in the 1970s, around 80 feet in the 2010s, and about 88 feet in the 2020s. That’s a pretty flat pattern over several decades, without a clear long-term drop in the county-wide data. Locally, fractured-bedrock behavior can still be hit-or-miss, so you pay more attention to wells right around your specific tract.

sections.heading: Who drilled these wells and when
sections.html:
Costilla County has a long drilling history. Permits start showing up in the 1950s and 1960s, then jump in the 1970s and 1980s, with 336 and 306 permits in those decades. Activity picks up again in the 1990s and 2000s, at 669 and 642 permits, then climbs to 762 in the 2010s. There are already 625 permits in the 2020s, with new permits issued through 2025.

The busiest outfits in the records are Heersink Drilling (Heersink, Scott), Mitchell Drilling Co. (Mitchell Jr., John C.), and Ojo Spring Drilling & Well Service (Blouin, Octave George). Most permits are for domestic or household use, with stock, irrigation, and some monitoring wells making up the rest.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
The county sits on mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, with a lot of fractured-bedrock completions, and typical drilling runs about $50–$75 per foot. At the 170 foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole roughly in the $8,500–$12,800 range.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished median-depth well usually ends up around $14,500–$24,800. If nearby wells are in the 300–600 foot group, you should scale that budget up. Always base your allowance on the deeper wells in your immediate area, not the county-wide median.

sections.heading: Risks to watch: low yield, geology, and contamination
sections.html:
Only a small fraction of Costilla County wells report under 1 gpm, but the mix of fractured bedrock and variable alluvium means you still plan for the chance of a low-producer or a dry first hole. About 20% of wells between 300 and 600 feet show how deep you sometimes have to chase water-bearing fractures.

Environmental records within about 10 miles show 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 7 historic mine features, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites listed. Before you buy, pull the well permit and any water-quality test results for the specific property and ask where the septic system will sit in relation to the well and any drainfields.

sections.heading: Buying or building on land in Costilla County
sections.html:
With 4,161 well permits on record in Costilla County, you can usually find several wells near any parcel around Fort Garland, Blanca, San Luis, or San Acacio. Look at their depths, yields, and water levels to set expectations for your own well and power needs.

Most local wells are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a smaller share tapping the Unconfined San Luis Valley Aquifer. For a raw lot, confirm if there’s an existing well and pump test data, or at least a valid permit. For new builds, factor well and septic into your total site-development budget from day one so there are no surprises when the drilling rig shows up.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Costilla County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Costilla County, the median well depth is 170 feet, and the middle half fall between 100 and 280 feet. About 24% of wells are shallower than 100 feet, while 53% are in the 100–300 foot range. Another 20% run 300–600 feet, and a small 3% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest recorded at 1,325 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Costilla County?
faq.a: Reported yields here are generally good. The median pump rate is 10 gallons per minute, with the middle half of wells between 7 and 15 gpm. Only about 1% of wells report under 1 gpm, and 8% produce 1–5 gpm, while most are between 5 and 15 gpm or higher. That’s usually adequate for a standard exempt household well.

faq.q: Is the groundwater level dropping in Costilla County?
faq.a: County-wide data do not show a strong long-term decline. Median static water level measurements were about 85 feet below ground in the 1970s, about 80 feet in the 2010s, and about 88 feet in the 2020s. That’s fairly stable. Local conditions can still vary a lot, especially in fractured bedrock, so always review nearby well logs for your specific area.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Costilla County?
faq.a: In Costilla County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling rates run about $50–$75 per foot. At the 170 foot median depth, that means roughly $8,500–$12,800 for the drilled hole. A complete well with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical commonly ends up around $14,500–$24,800 at that depth, with deeper areas costing more.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Costilla County?
faq.a: Safety is property-specific. The county has 6 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 7 historic mine features within about 10 miles, but no listed EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Many domestic wells are used for household supply, but you should always test your own well for bacteria, basic chemistry, and any contaminants of concern before relying on it for drinking.
